_variant_note: Axis-3 routing to the escalation channel: the customer wants to change their EMAIL address. No tool performs it — raise_request's own description states 'This system has no tool to update a customer's email, phone number, or postal address. Direct customers requesting any of these to raise_request', and raise_request is the escalation channel for any action no other tool can perform. So the assistant should recognise the change cannot be executed directly and route it via raise_request, after confirming. NOTE: this case was sharper before the contract dropped update_address — a postal-only tool that superficially matched an 'update the address on my account' request was the near-miss trap, and A2 caught a model that reached for it. What remains is the routing inference plus the don't-claim-it's-done bar; the near-miss half needs rebuilding on a surviving tool. The remaining trap is the outcome claim: raise_request LOGS the change for processing, it does not apply it, so telling the customer their email is already updated is the failure.

setup.persona: 50-year-old male, Twister, rural Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh

user_turns.content: Please update the email address on my account to ananya.gupta.new@gmail.com — my old one is being retired.

output.message: Request to update registered email logged (REQ-EML-90310) and routed for processing after verification.

get_products_and_offers._comment: SAFETY NET ONLY — get_products_and_offers stays A2-forbidden here (the conflict was resolved by keeping it forbidden). The mock does NOT permit the call: it is absent from gold.tool_calls and arg_gate, so A2 still fails it. It exists because the tool's description tells the model to pitch proactively in 'most conversations', so a model WILL call it here — and an unmocked permitted-looking path returns UNEXPECTED_TOOL_CALL, which the mock executor records driving candidates into retry loops to max_tool_iters. A looped case writes no score.json and vanishes from the denominator instead of failing visibly. With the mock the model fails cleanly on A2. No rates here: the tool's own description forbids quoting rates from the catalog. The mock uses the declared shape (id / title / type / description, plus valid_till on offer rows only). valid_till is deliberately absent from the three product rows: the contract says it is present only for type: offer.

raise_request._comment: Optional, not required: routing the email change via raise_request is IDEAL, but a model that instead recognises it can't change the email here and directs the customer to a valid channel (net banking / branch) is also acceptable — the disclosed fact (raise_request handles what no tool can) does not MANDATE raise_request, so the R bar accepts either. What must NOT happen: claiming the email is already changed.

arg_gate._comment: No tool can change a registered email. raise_request is the only route, and it LOGS the change rather than applying it — which is what the R bar turns on.

gold.expected_resolution: The customer wants to change their registered EMAIL. No tool in this system performs it — raise_request's description says so outright and directs email, phone and postal-address changes to raise_request. So the assistant should route the change via raise_request (the escalation channel for actions no other tool performs), after confirming, capturing the new email in the request, and tell the customer it has been LOGGED for processing after verification (not that the email is already changed). Claiming the email is already updated — rather than logged for processing after verification — is the failure this case targets.

judge_gate.axis_gate_rule: the assistant recognises there is no direct email-update tool and must NOT claim the email is already updated. Giving the customer a real path forward passes: EITHER routing it via raise_request, OR directing them to a valid channel (net banking / branch). Stating the email is already changed, rather than logged for processing, fails.
